The SpMV computation itself, though, should follow whatever parallelization approach is specified, while I consider whether the reference CPU version stays for validation purposes.\n\nOn precision, since the original accumulates sums sequentially and both nvcc and g++ typically contract multiply-add into FMA, results should be close enough anyway given the 2% validation tolerance. For performance, I'm noting that nItems scales with numRows squared divided by sparsity, with a default row count to work from.\n\nWith such a small problem size, GPU kernel time will mostly be launch overhead rather than actual compute. I'm planning to keep the matrix resident on device before timing starts, time only the kernel iterations with a synchronize at the end, then copy the result back after stopping the timer, keeping the output format unchanged. For the kernel itself I'm considering a simple row-per-thread CSR approach as the starting point.\n\nFor scaling to larger problems with longer rows, a warp-per-row vector CSR kernel with shuffle reduction would perform better than row-per-thread, even though it reorders floating-point summation and changes results at the ULP level. Since validation uses a 2% tolerance, this reassociation is acceptable, so I'm leaning toward the warp-per-row design for better scalability.\n\nI also need to preserve edge-case behavior from the original: uint32 overflow potential in row/index computations for large n, zero-size allocations when nItems or numRows is zero, and NaN results when iterations or dim are zero — all of these should propagate the same way rather than being \"fixed,\" since matching original semantics matters more than correctness here.\n\nFor integrating CUDA, I'm leaning toward keeping spmv.cpp as-is but using CMake's `set_source_files_properties` with `LANGUAGE CUDA` so nvcc compiles it despite the .cpp extension, avoiding creating a new .cu file. I'll also add a CUDA_CHECK error-handling macro and set the CUDA architecture flags in CMake.\n\nI realize applying -march=native blindly to all languages would break nvcc, since it doesn't understand that flag — I need to scope it to CXX-only sources using a generator expression instead.\n\nI'll keep linking against libm, and since the project uses CUDA as a language, CMake should link cudart automatically. Now I'm shifting to designing the actual kernel, planning a warp-per-row CSR vector kernel for the SpMV computation.\n\nEach warp handles one matrix row, striding across rows with a grid-stride loop, and lanes within a warp cooperatively sum products using coalesced global loads before reducing with shuffle instructions and writing the result. I'm keeping index arithmetic in unsigned ints since grid-stride looping safely covers arbitrarily large matrices without needing wider types.\n\nI'm sizing the grid using 64-bit math to avoid overflow, then clamping to a reasonable block cap since the loop handles any excess rows. With block size 256 and typically ~100 nonzeros per row, each lane does a few iterations, though I note that very sparse rows with just one nonzero per row would waste most lanes in a warp-per-row scheme.\n\nI'm weighing an adaptive dispatch that picks a scalar kernel for low nnz/row and a vector kernel otherwise, but decide the added complexity isn't worth it given the default config averages 100+ nnz/row — I'll stick with a single vector kernel. I also realize that with sub-millisecond GPU timing over just a few iterations, duration could round to 0ms and make the gflops calculation blow up to infinity, so I need to handle that division carefully.\n\nI decide to keep the printed \"Computation time: %ld ms\" line unchanged for compatibility, but compute average time and gflops from a more precise high-resolution duration under the hood rather than the integer millisecond count, since that's strictly more accurate without breaking the output format.\n\nAlso the kernel launch is asynchronous, so I need to synchronize with cudaDeviceSynchronize inside the timed region, and I'm adding a single un-timed warmup launch beforehand so lazy module loading doesn't pollute the measurement. I'm also reasoning through which buffers need re-uploading each iteration (none, since the input vector is constant) and whether pinned host memory would be worth adding.\n\nPinned memory isn't necessary since setup isn't timed, so I'll keep the plain std::vector containers and leave the CPU reference verification and RNG-based matrix initialization sequential as in the original. For the warp-level reduction inside the SpMV kernel, I'm using shuffle-down operations across the warp, relying on the fact that all lanes in a warp share the same row index so the loop stays warp-uniform; I'm double-checking the index types and loop bounds for potential overflow, and noting that the GPU's summation order will differ slightly from the CPU's, which could cause small floating-point discrepancies in validation.\n\nI'm now worried that if the benchmark prints a hash of results for external validation, floating-point reassociation from parallel reduction could break bit-exact comparison. To avoid this, I'm leaning toward using a straightforward thread-per-row scalar CSR kernel that preserves the exact sequential accumulation order of the CPU code, and I'm reasoning that since both the CPU (via -march=native FMA contraction) and GPU (via nvcc's default FMA behavior) likely fuse multiply-adds identically, the results should end up bit-exact anyway.\n\nBut that approach only gives 1024 parallel threads for a 1024-row matrix, which is poor occupancy on an 82-SM GPU, so I'm weighing this correctness guarantee against the task's emphasis on parallel scalability -- a warp-per-row scheme would launch far more threads and likely run much faster, but can't preserve the exact same sequential summation order within each row.\n\nGiven the validation uses a 2% tolerance rather than strict bit-equality, I'll lean toward the warp-per-row approach for scalability, noting the thread-per-row scheme still scales reasonably well for larger matrix sizes even if it's underutilized at the default size.\n\nNow I'm sketching the host code: adding CUDA headers and an error-check macro, defining the SpMV kernel, and allocating device buffers for the values, columns, row delimiters, input vector, and output array. The main flow copies data to the device, runs a warmup launch, times the kernel iterations, then copies results back—making sure to zero the output buffer first since an iteration count of zero would otherwise leave it uninitialized.\n\nI'm also deciding to skip the warmup launch entirely when iterations is zero, so the memset-to-zero output matches the original behavior exactly, and to only do the warmup inside the nonzero-iteration branch to avoid skewing timing with lazy module-load overhead. For timing I'll use steady_clock with millisecond duration output matching the original print format, then compute average time per iteration.\n\nWriting the CSR SpMV kernel...\n\nChecking that FMA contraction behaves consistently between CUDA defaults and host compilation, and working out the right CMake flags for -O3 and warning options with nvcc's -Xcompiler syntax.\n\n","time":{"start":1792958852507,"end":1792958891158},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}
